vignette:
Eleanor is 77 years old, a widow and a retired school counselor who spent forty years working in the same suburban high school. Three years ago, on an ordinary March afternoon, a former student walked into the building with a hunting rifle and began firing down the main corridor. Eleanor was in her office when the fire alarm sounded, a prearranged signal for lockdown. She guided a group of panicking students into a supply closet, held the door shut, and listened for what felt like an hour to the muffled pops and the screaming that finally stopped when police brought the shooter down in the gymnasium. No one in her immediate group was physically hurt, but she saw the body of a colleague being carried out on a stretcher. In the weeks that followed, the district offered counseling, and Eleanor initially thought she would be fine—she had spent her career helping others process trauma.

But she could not stop thinking about the shooter. During quiet moments, she found herself running through scenarios of what she would do if she ever faced him again, going over every detail of that afternoon and imagining ways to get even. This rumination had a rhythm: it began with a sharp memory of the sound of the gunshots, then escalated into a full mental courtroom where she argued that what happened to her was deeply unfair and that nothing had been done to make it right. The shooter had been wounded and arrested, but the trial ended in a plea deal that gave him a sentence Eleanor considered far too short. The injustice of it consumed her, and she began drinking a glass of wine in the early afternoon to quiet the spinning thoughts—then two, then sometimes a third before dinner. She had never been more than a social drinker before; now the habit felt necessary, a way to stop the loop of anger and helplessness. But the alcohol only made her feel more disconnected from the person she used to be. She used to be a happy, optimistic woman who found meaning in her work. Now she told herself she did not know herself anymore.

The drinking also made her sleep uneasily, and she would wake in the dark, breath held, sure she had heard something downstairs. She began listening for sounds that might mean someone was entering her home—a creak, a draft, the brush of a coat against the doorframe. Ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, like the hum of the refrigerator cycling on or a car door slamming two blocks away, made her jump. She could not relax even when she knew she was safe, sitting in her own living room with the deadbolt locked. She had come to believe that the world was fundamentally dangerous, that safety was an illusion, and that her own hypervigilance was the only thing keeping her alive. This belief deepened every time she startled at a sudden noise, because the fear itself felt like proof that danger was near. She felt trapped in a loop: the more she scanned for threats, the more she encountered them; the more she encountered them, the more convinced she became that the world had changed forever and that the happy, trusting person she had been was gone for good.

The avoidance was subtle but relentless. She stopped going to the grocery store at dusk, because the parking lot reminded her of the school lot at 3:15 that afternoon. She always chose a seat with a clear view of the door at the diner where she ate lunch a few days a week, and she made sure to sit close to an exit. This habit made her feel vaguely ashamed—she was a professional who had taught students how to manage fear—but the shame only added another layer to her misery. On the rare evenings she visited her daughter, she would walk the perimeter of the house before entering, checking windows and the back gate, and she could see the worry on her daughter's face. She had stopped talking about the shooting with anyone except to say she was fine. The silence was a strategy too: if she did not speak about it, maybe the memories would stay contained. But they did not. They grew louder, and her drinking increased, and she found herself crying without knowing why.

What finally brought Eleanor to ask for help was a moment of public embarrassment. At a retirement party for a former colleague, someone set off a balloon that popped loudly, and she dropped her plate, covered her ears, and shouted before she could stop herself. The room went silent. She left early and sat in her car, shaking, convinced that everyone now saw her as broken. That night she poured out the last of the wine and called a counselor she had once recommended to a student. She is terrified that she will never feel like herself again, but she is also tired—tired of being afraid in her own home, tired of the anger that feels like a second full-time job. In her first session, she said, "I just want to know if I can ever stop listening for the footsteps."
